ai_context.summary: A file the viewer names becomes something to open or locate rather than a string to copy, and a command's result becomes a translated panel instead of raw stdout -- both without a new dependency or an open execution surface.
ai_context.use when: Deciding how the viewer presents a file reference or the result of a command it can run.

Acceptance criteria: - AC1: Every place the viewer labels a file reference calls it `file`, not `path`, in both catalogues, and no label reads `path` where a file is meant.

- AC2: Every file reference the viewer shows (report Input, report Output/Artefact, render provenance, and any other) offers the same three controls -- Open, Copy path, Reveal -- rendered as icons with no visible text label, each carrying an accessible name resolved from the string catalogue.

- AC3: On a served page, Open launches the file through the host system's default handler and Reveal opens the containing folder with the file selected where the platform supports it; both are verified on the platform under test and the platforms not verified are stated as unverified.

- AC4: On a page opened from disk, Copy path behaves exactly as it does today and Open and Reveal are not offered as controls that appear to work -- absent or explicitly shown as unavailable, never silently inert.

- AC5: A decision is recorded (an amendment to adr_007 or a new ADR) covering how a file reaches the server without an operator-supplied path becoming a subprocess argument, and the implementation matches it.
- AC6: No `blender <path>` command is offered for copying anywhere in the viewer; opening a report's artefact goes through the Open control of AC2.
Needs: - Wherever the viewer shows a file it calls it `path` and prints the path itself -- a single copy-to-clipboard button carrying the whole string (report Input, report Output/Artefact, render provenance). The operator's actual intent is almost never 'I want this string': it is 'open this file', 'show me where it sits', and only sometimes 'give me the text'. One control serves the rarest of the three.

- The render panel offers `blender <path>` as a command to copy and paste into a terminal. Opening a .blend file is what the host system's file association already does; asking the operator to open a terminal to do it is a longer route to the same place.

- `List operations` and `Check setup` run for real on a served page (adr_007) but their result is dumped as raw process stdout into a `<pre>` inside the still-open menu dropdown: untranslated, unstyled, and shown in a container sized for a menu row. `Check setup` in particular prints a JSON object at the operator.

- Both rows sit in menus that do not describe them: `List operations` under File and `Check setup` under File, while both are reference material about the tool and its environment rather than actions on the current project.

ai_context.keywords: server-sent events, mtime signature poll, payload route, module split by screen, line budget, pytest layout, adr_004 amendment
ai_context.skip when: Deciding what the viewer displays or what a report contains -- req_000 and adr_001 hold that.
ai_context.summary: The served page becomes a live view onto the reports directory instead of a build-time snapshot, and both sides of the viewer gain a module structure, a checked size budget and a real test layout.
ai_context.use when: Deciding how the viewer stays current, or how the viewer's code is divided and checked.

Acceptance criteria: - AC1: The served page's payload is fetched from the server rather than read from a build-time file, and a page opened from disk keeps working exactly as it does today from its generated fallback.
- AC2: A served page reflects a new, changed or removed report without the operator restarting the server or reloading the page, within a few seconds of the file landing.

- AC3: Change detection uses the standard library only -- no file-watching dependency -- and its cost is bounded so that an idle viewer does not consume a meaningful share of a core; the bound is stated and measured, not asserted.
- AC4: The event stream carries what changed, not the changed data, and the client refetches only the affected part; no code path in the client reloads the whole page on a data change.
- AC5: A client with no event-stream support still converges on fresh data through a self-throttling fallback, and neither path leaves a timer or a connection running after the page is closed.

- AC6: `adr_004` is amended (or superseded) to record that the auto-refresh it promised now exists and how, that the served page is now the default mode with the opened-from-disk one behind a flag, and the build step the client split requires -- with the rejected alternative named.
Needs: - `meshanvil view` builds and opens a page from disk by default and only serves behind `--serve`, so the mode that can refresh itself is the one nobody gets unless they ask. Every launch also starts a fresh server on port 0, so the address changes every time -- an open tab, a bookmark and a second `meshanvil view` all point somewhere that no longer exists, and nothing notices that a viewer for this project is already running.

- `adr_004` states that `meshanvil view --serve` starts a server `for auto-refresh`. Nothing auto-refreshes: there is no watcher, no event stream and no polling anywhere in `meshanvil/viewer.py` or `viewer/viewer.js`. The promise is documented and was never built, so an operator watching a chain run has to stop the server, re-run the command and reopen the page to see the report that just landed.

- Even a manual browser refresh shows nothing new: the payload is baked into `work/viewer/data.js` at build time, so the page is a snapshot of the moment the command ran rather than a view onto the reports directory.

- `viewer/viewer.js` is 908 lines in one file covering every screen, every renderer and every event handler. Each slice that touches the viewer -- and the last four have -- edits the same file, and nothing states when it has grown too large.

- `meshanvil/viewer.py` is 199 lines doing three unrelated jobs: computing the payload, serving it over HTTP, and launching a browser. It is the file the next three endpoints (a data route, an event stream, and the open/reveal route `req_009_turn_the_viewer_s_file_references_and_command_rows_into_direct_translated_controls` needs) would all land in.

- There is no test directory and no test runner. `scripts/selfcheck.py` is 353 lines of hand-rolled asserts covering the whole host codebase in one file, so a single module's behaviour has nowhere of its own to be checked and a failure names the script rather than the unit.
